entities.summary:
Émile Noël (1922–1996) stands as a foundational architect of the European Union's institutional framework, serving as the first and longest-serving Secretary-General of the Commission of the European Economic Community (EEC) and its successor, the European Commission, from 1958 to 1987. Born in Istanbul, Noël, a French civil servant, dedicated nearly three decades to shaping the nascent European project from an ambitious post-war vision into a robust, integrated political and economic entity. His tenure spanned critical periods of expansion and deepening integration, including the initial establishment of the Common Market, the accession of new member states, and significant treaty reforms.

As Secretary-General, Noël was the administrative backbone of the European Commission, responsible for coordinating its sprawling bureaucracy and ensuring the effective implementation of European policies. He worked closely with successive Commission Presidents, including Walter Hallstein and Jacques Delors, navigating complex political landscapes and internal challenges. His contributions were particularly crucial during the formative years, where he helped define the Commission's role, establish its working methods, and foster a cohesive European civil service. He played a discreet but decisive role in the daily functioning of the European Communities, facilitating inter-institutional dialogue and preparing key legislative initiatives.
